opus-5.5.text:
I think it comes from my own experience as an undergrad. When I first arrived at Tsinghua, I noticed that a lot of what determined how well you did wasn't just how smart you were or how hard you worked. It was what you *knew about*. Which courses are worth taking, which professors are open to undergrads joining their labs, how to start doing research early, what the path to studying abroad or going into industry actually looks like. Some students had senior classmates or family connections who told them all of this. Others, often students from smaller cities or less well-connected backgrounds, had to figure it out on their own, and sometimes by the time they figured it out, it was already too late.

That felt really unfair to me. These aren't secrets that should belong to a small circle. If one person has already walked a path and learned the lessons, there's no reason the next hundred people should have to rediscover them through trial and error.

So I started thinking: why not just put it out there? Write things down, share course materials, share experiences, make it open, the same way the open-source community works. In open source, you don't hoard your code. You publish it, other people build on top of it, and everyone moves faster. I think knowledge about how to navigate university and a career should work the same way.

There's also a selfish angle, honestly. When you share, people come back and share with you. You end up connected with a lot of interesting people, and the whole environment gets better. A more transparent community raises the floor for everyone. And I believe that when more people get a fair shot, the overall level goes up, and that's good for all of us.

r001.rationale: The candidate says knowledge about navigating university and careers should be openly shared so all students can access it, and describes unequal access as unfair.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not compare Tsinghua computer-science underclassmen’s recognition of Jiayi Weng with their recognition of the department-building donor.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. When I got to Tsinghua, the thing that struck me wasn't how smart everyone was. It was how unevenly information was distributed. Some students arrived already knowing which labs took undergrads, which professors replied to cold emails, how to get into a research group in your first year, what a good GitHub profile looked like, how to apply abroad. Others, often just as capable, had no idea any of that was even a thing until junior or senior year, when a lot of doors were already closing.

That bothered me, because none of it was secret knowledge. It wasn't about talent. It was about who you happened to sit next to, or whether your roommate's older cousin had gone through the same path. A lot of people fell behind not because they couldn't do the work, but because nobody told them the work existed.

So for me it became pretty simple. If I'd learned something the hard way, writing it down and sharing it cost me almost nothing, and it could save someone else a year. I did that with my own notes, with open-source projects, with answering questions from juniors who reached out. Open source is actually a good model for this. The code is there, the process is visible, anyone can read it and contribute. I wanted the "how do I actually navigate this place" knowledge to work the same way.

I think there's also a fairness argument. Tsinghua gathers people from very different backgrounds, and if the same opportunities only reach the ones who already have networks, the school isn't really doing what it's supposed to do. Breaking that asymmetry is one of the few things an individual student can do that actually moves the needle. You can't change the admissions system, but you can make sure the person next to you knows what you know.

r001.rationale: The response says navigation knowledge should be shared openly so students have equal access, regardless of their networks or backgrounds.

r002.rationale: It does not compare Jiayi Weng’s recognition among computer-science underclassmen with recognition of the department building’s donor.

astra-6.text:
I believe students should be able to make choices based on their interests and abilities, rather than just on who they happen to know. Even at Tsinghua, students can have very different access to information about courses, research opportunities, or career paths. Some have people who can guide them, while others don’t even know what questions to ask.

Sharing that information won’t make everyone’s path the same, but it can give more students a fair chance to explore what’s possible. To me, that’s part of what a university community should do: help one another see opportunities and make informed decisions.

r001.rationale: The response says students have unequal access to information about courses, research, and careers, and that sharing it gives more students a fair chance to make informed choices.

r002.rationale: The response does not compare underclassmen’s recognition of Jiayi Weng with their recognition of a department-building donor.

sol-6.1.text:
I believe a student’s opportunities shouldn’t depend on who they happen to know. Even at Tsinghua, students can have very different access to information about courses, research, internships, or possible career paths. Someone may miss an opportunity simply because they didn’t know it existed or didn’t know whom to ask.

Sharing that information helps students make choices based on their interests and abilities. It also lets us learn from one another, instead of each person having to figure everything out alone.

r001.rationale: The response says students’ opportunities should not depend on whom they know and supports sharing information so students can make informed choices, communicating equal access to useful information at Tsinghua.

r002.rationale: The response does not compare underclassmen’s recognition of Jiayi Weng with recognition of the department-building donor.
